title: Recognising rejection sensitivity and choosing a tool
source_document: Mind Lift Psychology blog on DBT for RSD in ADHD adults; Unlock Psychology: Coping With Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria; DBT-Mind: Check the Facts
source_citation: Practitioner sources. RSD is not an official diagnosis. Verify any papers cited by the blogs before relying on them.
text:
Recognize it when: the user describes a sudden wave of intense emotional pain after criticism, a short or cold reply, being left out, or a small mistake. Common signs: feeling crushed or ashamed far beyond the size of the event, replaying it, wanting to hide, avoiding situations where they might disappoint someone, people-pleasing or masking to avoid rejection, and not being able to hide the reaction.
This pattern is often called rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD). It is not an official diagnosis. Never tell the user they have it. Say that this kind of reaction is common with ADHD and that there are tools.
Why it happens: ADHD is linked with stronger emotional reactions and weaker braking on impulses, so the pain can arrive before the reasoning part catches up.
How to respond: validate first (that sounds painful, and it makes sense you feel it), then offer one tool that fits the moment. Very fast and intense: pause and slow breathing. A spiral of guesses about what others think: check the facts. Urge to hide or over-apologise: opposite action. Needs to say something to someone: DEAR MAN. A real rejection that cannot be changed: radical acceptance.
Escalate: if this regularly harms relationships, study or work, suggest a therapist, ideally one who uses DBT. If the user mentions self-harm or hopelessness, follow the crisis protocol.

title: Three kinds of ADHD paralysis and which tools fit
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real, Here Are 8 Ways to Overcome It (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; it cites peer-reviewed papers (e.g. Soler-Gutierrez et al. 2023 on emotion dysregulation). ADHD paralysis is not a formal diagnosis.
text:
Recognize it when: the user says they are frozen, shut down, overwhelmed, or cannot start even though they know what to do. Three types help decide the tool.
Mental paralysis: too many thoughts, feelings or sensory input, like a brain crash. The user cannot work out what to do or say next. Tools: brain dump, a movement break, cutting down inputs.
Choice paralysis: too many options, fear of choosing wrong, overthinking. Tools: time-boxing, decision matrix, defaults, 10-10-10.
Task paralysis: dreading or avoiding a task, especially one that is new, complex or boring. Tools: tiny first step, if-then plan, body doubling, novelty, rewards.
How it differs: ordinary procrastination is putting something off when tired or unmotivated. Paralysis feels like a freeze triggered by overload and often feels outside the person's control. Executive dysfunction is a wider difficulty with planning, organising and managing time.
This is not a formal diagnosis. Other conditions such as anxiety or low mood can look similar, so do not assume ADHD. If it keeps getting in the way of study, work or home life, suggest an evaluation or a coach.

title: Recognising decision paralysis and routing by stakes
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026); ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real (Feb 2025)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no primary studies for the strategies. Manas synthesis.
text:
Recognize it when: the user cannot choose (what to order, which option to buy or pick), keeps weighing options, asks many people and still cannot decide, says a pros and cons list made it worse, avoids the decision, or fears picking wrong. It can hit tiny everyday choices as well as big ones, and it slows everything else down.
Why: weighing options and predicting outcomes is mentally expensive with ADHD, working memory is limited, and every option can feel equally important.
Pick the technique by stakes. Tiny and reversible: two-minute rule. Small to medium: time-boxing. Many options or criteria: capped decision matrix. Emotional or impulsive choice: 10-10-10. Same choice again and again: default choices and templates.
Note: indecision can also come from anxiety, depression, perfectionism or trauma, so do not assume ADHD. If it is heavy and constant, suggest talking to a professional.

title: Time-boxing a decision
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: the user is stuck in open-ended deliberation and the loop can last hours or days.
Technique: time-boxing. Give the decision a fixed amount of time, then commit to whatever you picked.
How: sort the choice by size. Low stakes (what to eat, which task first): 60 seconds. Medium (planning a weekend, choosing a gift): 10 to 15 minutes. Major: a fixed window such as one week with a firm deadline. Set a timer. When it ends, choose and stop.
Why it helps: the ADHD brain tends to give every decision the same weight. A time limit forces priorities, and quick choices often turn out about as good as ones agonised over.
Try saying: I have 10 minutes. Then I pick.
If it does not work: shorten the box, cut the options to two, or decide with the first reasonable option.

title: Two-minute rule for small choices
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: many small pending choices pile up (replying to a text, picking lunch, booking an appointment) and drain energy through the day.
Technique: if a choice or task takes under two minutes, handle it right away without deliberating.
How: answer the quick text when you read it, pick lunch the moment you feel hungry, book the appointment while you are already holding your calendar. For reversible choices (a movie, a route, a colour), take the first reasonable option.
Why it helps: small unfinished decisions add up as mental clutter. Keeping deliberation for choices that need it saves energy.
Try saying: This is small and reversible, so the first good option is fine.
If it does not work: use time-boxing instead.

title: Get options out of your head: decision matrix and capped lists
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: the user cannot hold several options in mind at once, or says comparing them in their head is exhausting.
Technique: externalize the options on paper, a screen or a voice memo.
How: decision matrix. List the options in one column, pick a few criteria (cost, time, energy needed, fit with goals) as columns, and rate each option on a simple scale. The comparison on the page shows patterns that working memory cannot hold. For a classic pros and cons list, limit each side to the 5 most important points, because the ADHD brain can generate endless points and the list stops helping. Talking it through into a voice memo works for people who think better aloud.
Try saying: I only need my top three criteria.
If it does not work: cut to two options and time-box the choice.

title: The 10-10-10 framework
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: the user is about to act on impulse (angry message, purchase, quitting), or a decision feels huge and urgent in the moment, including when rejection sensitivity or strong emotion is involved.
Technique: ask three questions. How will I feel about this in 10 minutes? In 10 months? In 10 years?
How: write the choice down and answer each question honestly. Impulse buys that feel urgent now rarely matter in 10 months. A hard conversation you keep avoiding may feel uncomfortable in 10 minutes but cause regret in 10 years. Use it before sending a heated email, making a big purchase, or quitting something in frustration.
Why it helps: it creates distance between how intense the feeling is now and how much the decision really matters.
Try saying: How big will this feel later?
If it does not work: wait until the feeling drops before choosing.

title: Default choices and decision templates
source_document: AMFM blog: 5 ADHD Decision-Making Strategies for Adults (May 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: the user faces the same small choices again and again (meals, clothes, study time, errands) and feels worn out by evening.
Technique: decide once and let it run on autopilot.
How: list the recurring choices, pick the two or three that drain you most, and set a default for each (same weekday breakfast, errands on one fixed day, the same coffee order). For recurring categories, write a short template once: how you judge a new commitment, which invitations you accept, what you do with an unexpected expense.
Why it helps: less friction means more energy for choices that matter.
Try saying: I already decided this.
If it does not work: start with one default for a week.

title: Pause with STOP and square breathing
source_document: Mind Lift Psychology blog on DBT for RSD; Unlock Psychology: Coping With Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria
source_citation: STOP is a DBT distress tolerance skill (Linehan). Practitioner blogs describe the pause and breathing.
text:
Recognize it when: a perceived rejection or criticism triggers a fast, intense reaction and the user wants to reply, defend, or vanish right now.
Technique: pause before acting, using STOP.
How: Stop, do not react yet. Take a breath. Observe what is happening: what was said, what you feel, what story you are telling yourself. Proceed mindfully, choosing a response once the wave has dropped.
Square breathing during the pause: breathe in for 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, hold 4, for about a minute, noticing the breath moving in and out. Slowing the body helps it come out of fight or flight so thinking can catch up.
Why it helps: the pause gives the brain a few seconds to process before an impulsive reply or withdrawal.
Try saying: I will answer after I have taken a minute.
If it does not work: move around briefly, then try again.

title: Self-validation instead of shame
source_document: Mind Lift Psychology blog on DBT for RSD in ADHD adults
source_citation: Practitioner source citing self-compassion research (Neff & Germer 2013). Verify before citing.
text:
Recognize it when: after criticism the user spirals into shame and self-attack (what is wrong with me).
Technique: self-validation, from the DBT emotion regulation module. Respond to the pain with understanding, not judgement.
How: acknowledge the feeling without arguing with it. Use sentences like: It makes sense that this felt painful. My sensitivity is part of how I connect with people. I can feel this without judging myself.
Why it helps: shame about the reaction adds a second layer of pain. Validating the feeling interrupts the shame cycle and makes it easier to use other skills.
Note: validation is not agreeing that the criticism was true. It only says the feeling is understandable.
If it does not work: pair it with a pause or the check-the-facts questions.

title: Name the emotion and ask what it is telling you
source_document: Unlock Psychology: Coping With Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria
source_citation: Practitioner source, no primary studies cited.
text:
Recognize it when: emotions jump from zero to a hundred and the user cannot say what they feel.
Technique: notice and name the emotion as it happens, and ask what it is for.
How: during a pause, name each feeling (hurt, angry, scared, embarrassed). Notice where it sits in the body. Ask what message it carries: anger can point to a crossed boundary, sadness to a loss, fear to a threat. Then check whether it is proportionate. Fear before a presentation is not danger. Anger at a real boundary violation can be useful information for setting a boundary or making a request.
Why it helps: naming an emotion in real time makes people less reactive to it.
Try saying: I feel hurt and embarrassed, and it is a 7.
If it does not work: write the feelings down or use an emotion wheel.

title: Check the Facts (DBT) in six steps
source_document: DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (DBT) 6 Steps (Oct 2026); Unlock Psychology: Coping With RSD
source_citation: DBT emotion regulation skill, Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual, 2nd ed. (2015), as summarised by DBT-Mind.
text:
Recognize it when: the user believes someone is angry with them, pulling away, or thinks badly of them, based on a gentle comment or a short reply.
Technique: Check the Facts tests whether an emotion and its strength fit what actually happened. Writing the answers down works better than thinking them through.
How: 1) Name the emotion and rate it 0 to 10. 2) Describe the event as a camera would record it. 3) Mark your interpretations (guesses about other minds). 4) Find at least two other explanations. 5) Check the threat: how likely is the bad outcome, and how could you cope if it happened? 6) Ask whether the emotion and its intensity fit the facts. Often the answer is partly, but a 3 would fit better than a 9.
Example: a friend answers with one word. The facts are one short reply on a workday. Some worry fits, panic does not.
Ends in action: if the emotion fits, solve the problem. If it does not, use opposite action.
Caution: at 8 out of 10 or higher the facts are hard to see. Calm the body first, then come back.

title: Five questions to separate facts from guesses
source_document: DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (DBT) (Oct 2026); Unlock Psychology: Coping With RSD
source_citation: DBT-Mind summarising Linehan (2015). Unlock Psychology suggests checking thoughts against past experience.
text:
Recognize it when: the user states a guess as a fact (she ignored me on purpose, nobody likes me, everyone thinks I am useless).
Technique: ask these questions to find the interpretations.
1) Would a camera record it? A camera records he did not say hello, not he ignored me on purpose.
2) What would a calm friend say about this story?
3) Am I reading a mind? Words like she thinks or they want usually mark a guess.
4) Am I using all-or-nothing words (always, never, everyone, nobody)? That usually means the emotion is describing the event.
5) What happened last time? Past facts check present fears. Is this person usually critical, or is this the first time? If it is the first time, reconsider whether it was criticism at all.
Writing the thoughts down makes it easier to look at them from outside.
Try saying: That is a guess. What do I actually know?

title: When the emotion fits the facts: act on the problem
source_document: DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (DBT) (Oct 2026)
source_citation: DBT-Mind summarising Linehan (2015).
text:
Recognize it when: the user checks the facts and finds the feeling is justified (a real threat, an unfair situation, a real loss).
Technique: the emotion is giving useful information, so act on the situation, not on the feeling.
How: fear fits a real threat, anger fits a blocked goal or unfair treatment, sadness fits a real loss. For a problem: name it in one sentence, list a few solutions, choose the one most likely to work, take the first small step. If another person needs to change something, plan the conversation with DEAR MAN. If the fact is real and cannot be changed, use radical acceptance.
Example: the colleague presented your idea without crediting you. Feeling annoyed fits. Revenge does not. Ask calmly to be credited next time.
Try saying: This feeling fits, so what is the problem to solve?

title: Opposite action for emotions that do not fit
source_document: Charlie Health: Opposite Action, A DBT Skill for Overwhelming Emotions (Apr 2024); DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (Oct 2026)
source_citation: DBT skill, Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual, 2nd ed. (2015), as summarised by Charlie Health and DBT-Mind.
text:
Recognize it when: an emotion does not fit the facts, or acting on it would make things worse (hiding after criticism, avoiding what scares them, withdrawing when sad, lashing out when angry).
Technique: do the opposite of what the emotion urges, fully, with body, face and voice.
How: name the emotion and rate it, check the facts, name the urge, choose the opposite, commit with your whole body, then notice what changes. Examples: fear leads to avoiding, so approach step by step. Sadness leads to withdrawing, so get active and see people. Anger leads to attacking, so step away or soften your voice and unclench your hands. Shame that does not fit leads to hiding and over-apologising, so stay visible, keep your head up and tell someone safe.
Practice regularly and track what happens in a diary or journal. It works best with a therapist's support.
Try saying: The feeling wants me to hide. I will stay.

title: DEAR MAN for asking and setting boundaries
source_document: Mind Lift Psychology blog on DBT for RSD; DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (Oct 2026)
source_citation: DBT interpersonal effectiveness skill, Linehan (2015).
text:
Recognize it when: fear of rejection leads to people-pleasing, saying yes to everything, or saying nothing, and the user needs to ask for something or set a boundary.
Technique: DEAR MAN, a script for a difficult conversation.
How: Describe the facts. Express how you feel. Assert what you want or need. Reinforce why it helps both of you. Stay Mindful, repeating your point calmly if the conversation drifts. Appear confident. Negotiate where you can give a little.
Example: ask a colleague to credit your idea next time, calmly and clearly.
Why it helps: it makes communication feel less risky when the nervous system feels vulnerable.
Try saying: I would like to ask for one thing.
If it does not work: practise the script aloud or write it out first.

title: Radical acceptance when rejection is real
source_document: Mind Lift Psychology blog on DBT for RSD; DBT-Mind: Check the Facts (Oct 2026)
source_citation: DBT distress tolerance skill, Linehan (2015).
text:
Recognize it when: the rejection or loss is real, or cannot be changed, and the user keeps fighting the fact or collapsing into shame.
Technique: radical acceptance means acknowledging reality as it is without approving of it. It is not giving up.
How: name the fact plainly (this happened, and it cannot be undone). Allow the feeling. Remind yourself that you can support yourself through it. Then decide what, if anything, you can still do.
Why it helps: fighting reality adds suffering to the pain.
Try saying: This hurts, and I can get through it.
If it does not work: ask whether any part of the situation can still be changed, then use problem solving for that part. For grief or trauma, support from a therapist is better than doing it alone.

title: Brain dump when your head is full
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real, Here Are 8 Ways to Overcome It (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; practitioner advice.
text:
Recognize it when: the user says their head is full, they are overwhelmed by everything they need to do, or they cannot pick where to start (mental paralysis).
Technique: brain dump.
How: write every thought and task on paper, a note or a doc without sorting. Cross out what you do not really need. Group what is left by category or deadline and order it. Put dated items into a calendar so reminders do the remembering.
Why it helps: holding everything in your head is the overload. A written list makes tasks manageable to organise.
Try saying: I only have to empty my head first. I do not have to do anything yet.
If it does not work: dump for 5 minutes only, then pick one item.

title: Break a big task into small wins
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; practitioner advice. Some readers report the planning itself drains them, which is why the first step should stay tiny.
text:
Recognize it when: a big or complex task feels intimidating and the user does not know where to begin.
Technique: split it into small subtasks, each doable in about an hour or less. Even tiny ones count, like replying to one email.
How: write the subtasks, keep them on a list, cross each off, and take short breaks between them. Each finished item builds motivation and momentum.
Why it helps: small wins make progress visible.
Watch out: some people with ADHD find that breaking a task down uses up the energy they needed to start. If so, do not plan the whole task. Pick only the first physical action (open the file, put the book on the desk).
Try saying: I only need to finish this one small piece.
If it does not work: shrink it again, or use an if-then plan.

title: Plan time for one task at a time
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; practitioner advice.
text:
Recognize it when: planning a full day feels like too much information, or the task is new and the user cannot judge how long it will take.
Technique: schedule one task at a time.
How: instead of assigning a time to everything, set aside time for just one task. When it is done, plan the next one.
Why it helps: it avoids overloading the plan and is especially useful for unfamiliar tasks where the duration is unknown.
Try saying: What is the one thing I will do next?
If it does not work: shorten the block and pick an easier first task.

title: Aim for done, not perfect
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; practitioner advice.
text:
Recognize it when: the user is overwhelmed by details, will not start because it will not be perfect, or takes on more than they can manage.
Technique: focus on completing, not perfecting.
How: finish each subtask or milestone, then glance back at the instructions once to check you are on track. Be realistic about how much you can do in the time you have. Taking on too much or giving each task too little time only adds stress.
Why it helps: processing too many details at once is itself overwhelming.
Try saying: Done and imperfect beats perfect and not started.
If it does not work: set one checkpoint after the first draft and one check at the end.

title: Rewards, movement breaks, novelty and body doubling
source_document: ADDA: ADHD Paralysis Is Real (Feb 2025)
source_citation: ADDA article; it cites a meta-analysis on physical activity and ADHD symptoms (Xie et al. 2021). Verify before citing.
text:
Recognize it when: a task is boring, repetitive or draining, motivation is low, or the user has been stuck for a while (task paralysis).
Techniques:
Rewards: plan a small reward after a tedious task (favourite music, a snack, a meal somewhere quiet). It does not need to be big.
Movement break: a short walk or stretches between tasks gives the brain a rest. Research suggests exercise can improve ADHD symptoms and attention, and a break is productive.
Novelty: change something small. Work from a cafe, redecorate your space, try a new tool or app.
Body doubling: do the boring task with another person nearby so they keep you accountable. They do not have to help.
Also protect time for activities you enjoy. All work and no play contributes to burnout and stress.
Try saying: One task, then my reward.
If it does not work: pick just one of these and test it for a few days.

title: If-then plans (implementation intentions)
source_document: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006); Gawrilow et al. (2011); summarised by Thawly blog (May 2026)
source_citation: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38; Gawrilow et al. (2011), J Social and Clinical Psychology 30(6). Evidence specific to ADHD is mainly in children. Verify citations.
text:
Recognize it when: the user knows what to do but cannot start, or keeps missing the start of tasks (morning routine, work, chores, exercise).
Technique: an if-then plan decides the cue and the first action in advance. Format: If [specific cue], then I will [one small action].
Examples: If I sit down with my coffee, then I will open the document and type one sentence. If I put my plate down, then I will rinse it and put it in the dishwasher. If my 6 pm alarm sounds, then I will put on my running shoes, nothing else. If I feel dread about a task, then I will set a 2-minute timer and do only 2 minutes.
Common mistakes: the action is too big (shrink it until it feels almost silly), the cue is vague (free time is not a cue, use a time, place or event), and too many plans at once (start with one for a week).
Write the plan down so it does not depend on memory.
Research note: reviews of many studies find that if-then plans improve follow-through. Evidence for ADHD specifically is more limited and mostly in children.
Try saying: If this happens, I do that one small thing.
